title: Running more than three kilometers during the first week of a running regimen may be associated with increased risk of injury in obese novice runners
authors: Nielsen RO, Bertelsen ML, Parner ET, Sorensen H, Lind M, Rasmussen S
journal: International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy
population: Healthy novice runners, 749 of 1532 eligible volunteers, BMI at most 30 versus above 30
findings: 3-week observational explorative prospective cohort; runners were stratified by BMI (30 or less = low; above 30 = high) and week-1 distance (under 3 km, 3 to 6 km, over 6 km); 56 runners were injured.
BMI above 30 with 3 to 6 km in week 1: cumulative risk difference +14.3% (95% CI 3.3 to 25.3, p<0.01) versus the low-BMI, low-distance reference.
BMI above 30 with over 6 km in week 1: CRD +16.2% (95% CI 4.4 to 28.0, p<0.01).
The additive interaction between high distance and BMI was positive but not significant (11.7%, 95% CI -3.6 to 27.0, p=0.13).
Number of obese runners who would need to change from high to low week-1 distance to avoid one injury: 8.5 (95% CI 4.6 to 52).
Conclusion: individuals with BMI above 30 may be well advised to begin with an initial distance under 3 km (1.9 miles) in the first week; large-scale trials are needed. Level of evidence 2b.
limitations: Exploratory; only 749 of 1532 eligible runners volunteered; week-1 distance was self-chosen (not randomised, so confounded by who chooses to run far); 3-week window; interaction term not significant; the paper gives a weekly distance, not a per-session dose. No DOI is registered for this record (PubMed and PMC4060311 only).
implications: Cap week-1 running at under 3 km for BMI above 30; scale the floor dose by BMI rather than using one number (grade C).
The paper gives a week-1 total, not a session split; any per-session figure (for example 3 sessions under 1 km) is the plan's own arithmetic.
The BMI scaler should apply in the first 1 to 3 weeks only, since the data cover 3 weeks.
